object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triage-stage event tracked by the organization; the central unit of work for handling outages/problems.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, formatted INC- plus a sequence, never reused.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform (automatic or manually raised) that something may be wrong.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Identifier for an alert, issued by the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, potentially linked to an incident as its origin.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact/blast-radius classification of an incident, one of SEV1-SEV4.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer-urgency classification of an incident, one of P1-P4, independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can act as an incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns a service on a standing basis.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A catalogued system/service that can be affected by incidents and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate chains (C duplicates B, B duplicates A) are described as 'wrong' but 'not enforced' -- should this be modeled as a hard acyclic/transitive-collapse constraint (every duplicate must point directly at a non-duplicate primary), or left as an unenforced business rule/data-quality issue? Current model only captures irreflexivity and per-incident single-primary cardinality, not the 'no chains' rule, since it isn't system-enforced.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? ... It's wrong. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are modeled as attributes holding only the 'current' value, per facilitator's decision, but both are explicitly stated to change over time with history kept in a separate 'timeline' concept not described in this transcript. source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Commander mandatory participation is conditional on incident state (mandatory only when state = 'declared' or later; none in 'triage'). Standard ORM mandatory constraints don't capture conditional/state-dependent mandatory participation cleanly -- this may require a subtype (e.g., DeclaredIncident subtype of Incident) to express precisely, which was not created here to avoid inventing an unstated identification scheme.

source_references.excerpt: A commander is assigned when it's declared. ... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

source_references.excerpt: Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. ... And people say "sev" when they mean either.

ambiguities.description: 'Owner'/'owns' is used ambiguously in conversation for both Service Owner (team, standing) and Incident Commander (person, per-incident) -- explicitly flagged by stakeholders as genuinely ambiguous in casual usage ('who owns this?'). The model resolves this via two distinct fact types, but real-world usage/reporting may still conflate them.
